tldr: The paper proposes CAST (Chunking via Abstract Syntax Trees), a structure-aware chunking method for RAG pipelines that recursively splits and merges AST nodes to produce semantically coherent code chunks, improving both retrieval and generation performance across multiple benchmarks.
contributions: CAST: an AST-based recursive split-then-merge chunking algorithm that preserves syntactic integrity and maximizes information density
Demonstration of improved retrieval (Recall@5 +4.3 on RepoEval) and generation (Pass@1 +2.67 on SWE-bench) performance
Cross-language consistency showing up to 4.3-point gains on CrossCodeEval
Metadata retention benefits for hybrid code+natural language tasks
methods: Source code is parsed into ASTs using the tree-sitter library. A recursive, split-then-merge algorithm traverses the tree top-down, greedily fitting large AST nodes into chunks when possible; nodes exceeding the size limit are recursively broken into smaller children. Adjacent small sibling nodes are then merged to maximize per-chunk information density. Chunk size is measured by non-whitespace character count rather than lines, with max_context_length set to 4000 for RepoEval and SWE-Bench and 10000 for CrossCodeEval.
results: CAST improves Retrieval@5 by 4.3 points on RepoEval and Pass@1 by 2.67 points on SWE-bench. StarCoder2-7B sees an average 5.5-point gain on RepoEval. Precision gains range from 1.2-3.3 points and Recall from 1.8-4.3 points on RepoEval across all retrievers. On NL-to-code retrieval (SWE-Bench), gains are 0.5-1.4 in Precision and 0.7-1.1 in Recall. CrossCodeEval shows up to 4.3-point gains with largest improvements on TypeScript. Merging ablations show both retrieval and generation decline under split-only strategies.
limitations: Lacks explicit contextual awareness from higher chunking units in the AST hierarchy
Only explores chunking with pure code files, without multi-view inputs like comments, natural language descriptions, or pseudo code
Relies on static AST analysis only, without execution traces, type inference, or compilation awareness for per-query adaptiveness
